title: Middleware, Context, and Tests
summary: Wrap every request in middleware, carry request-scoped values and deadlines in the context, and test the whole API in memory with httptest.
intro: Some work belongs to every request: an id to trace it, a log line, panic recovery, security headers, and the login check. In Go that's middleware, which passes what it learns to the handlers through the request's context. And because a whole API is one `http.Handler`, you can test it in memory with `httptest`, with no server and no network.

steps.title: Middleware

examples.title: The middleware chain
examples.prompt: Read `NewServer`, which wraps the routes in Taskboard's middleware. The output is the response to `GET /healthz` sent with `X-Request-ID: docs-1`.
examples.code:
// NewServer returns the whole API as one http.Handler: the routes of routes.go inside
// the middleware chain, listed here from the outside in.
func NewServer(deps Deps) http.Handler {
	s := &server{Deps: deps, logins: newLimiter(12*time.Second, 5)}
	mux := http.NewServeMux()
	s.routes(mux)

	h := s.unmatched(mux)
	h = s.crossOrigin(h)
	h = s.cors(h)
	h = secureHeaders(h)
	h = s.recoverPanics(h)
	h = measure(h)
	h = s.logRequests(h)
	h = countQueries(deps.Development)(h)
	h = requestID(h)
	return h
}
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Referrer-Policy: no-referrer
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
X-Query-Count: 0
X-Request-Id: docs-1
Date: Tue, 20 Oct 2026 01:43:59 GMT
Content-Length: 16

{"status":"ok"}
examples.explanation: Each line wraps everything built so far, so `requestID`, wrapped last, runs first, and `unmatched`, wrapped first, runs last, right before the mux. The order is deliberate: the request id exists before anything logs, and `recoverPanics` sits inside `logRequests`, so a panic still produces a logged 500. The health handler set only `Content-Type` and wrote `{"status":"ok"}`. The other headers came from middleware: the echoed `X-Request-Id`, the two security headers, and `X-Query-Count`, which counts database queries in development.

examples.title: A log line per request
examples.prompt: Read `logRequests`. The output is the line it logged for `GET /v1/tasks/3`.
examples.explanation: `statusRecorder` wraps `w` to note the status and byte count as the handler writes them. Everything after `next.ServeHTTP` runs once the handler is done, so the line has the final status and the real duration. `r.Pattern` (Go 1.23) is the route that matched, `GET /v1/tasks/{taskID}`, while `path` is the URL that was asked for. Group dashboards and alerts by pattern: grouped by path, every task id would be its own row. Bodies are never logged, because they can hold passwords.

steps.title: The request context
steps.body:
Every request carries a `context.Context`, `r.Context()`. It's canceled when the client disconnects or the server shuts down, so pass it as the first argument to every call that does I/O. pgx stops a query when its context ends, so a request nobody is waiting for stops using the database.

Middleware also uses the context to hand request-scoped values to handlers. `context.WithValue` returns a new context holding one value, and `r.WithContext` makes a request that carries it. Key each value with an unexported type, so no other package can read or overwrite it by accident:

```go
type requestIDKey struct{}
```

Keep context values to facts about this one request: its id, the logged-in user, the open transaction. Dependencies such as a logger or a store go through constructors. And when one call must not hang, give it a deadline of its own with `context.WithTimeout`, then `defer cancel()` right away.

examples.title: The user in the context
examples.prompt: Read `requireAuth`, the middleware in front of every private route. The output is the response to `GET /v1/tasks/3` sent with no token.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
Cache-Control: no-store
Content-Type: application/problem+json
Referrer-Policy: no-referrer
Www-Authenticate: Bearer realm="taskboard"
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
X-Query-Count: 0
X-Request-Id: 01a156fa-cd89-7b9d-ba97-8bb5909b3636
Date: Tue, 20 Oct 2026 01:43:59 GMT
Content-Length: 183

{"type":"about:blank","title":"Unauthorized","status":401,"detail":"unauthenticated: log in to continue","instance":"/v1/tasks/3","request_id":"01a156fa-cd89-7b9d-ba97-8bb5909b3636"}
examples.explanation: `requireAuth` finds the token, asks `AuthService.Authenticate` whose it is, and calls the next handler with a request whose context holds that user. `auth.WithUser` stores the user under an unexported key type, and `auth.UserFrom` reads it back, which is all the handlers' `user(r)` helper does. On failure it writes a 401 problem and returns without calling `next`, so the handler never runs. `WWW-Authenticate` tells the client which scheme to use.

examples.title: A deadline for one call
examples.prompt: Read `readyz`. The output shows two responses: one while the database was up, and one after it was stopped.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Referrer-Policy: no-referrer
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
X-Query-Count: 0
X-Request-Id: 01a156fa-cdee-7fca-90c0-89b53195a4ca
Date: Tue, 20 Oct 2026 01:43:59 GMT
Content-Length: 40

{"status":"ready","checks":{"db":"ok"}}

HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable
Content-Type: application/json
Referrer-Policy: no-referrer
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
X-Query-Count: 0
X-Request-Id: 01a156fa-d98b-7d58-94e6-f5d6c612eead
Date: Tue, 20 Oct 2026 01:44:02 GMT
Content-Length: 47

{"status":"not_ready","checks":{"db":"error"}}
examples.explanation: A load balancer calls `/readyz` every few seconds and sends traffic only while it answers 200, so the check must answer fast even when the database doesn't. `context.WithTimeout` derives a context that ends after one second, or sooner if the request's own context ends, and `defer cancel()` releases its timer as soon as the handler returns. `errors.Is(err, context.DeadlineExceeded)` tells a timeout from other failures. Here the database had been stopped, so the ping failed at once with an error, not a timeout. `/healthz` never touches the database, so a slow database can't get a healthy process restarted.

steps.title: Testing handlers with httptest
steps.body:
A whole API is one `http.Handler`, so a test can call it directly, with no server and no port:

```go
rec := httptest.NewRecorder()
routes().ServeHTTP(rec, httptest.NewRequest("GET", tc.path, nil))
```

`httptest.NewRequest` builds a request, and `httptest.NewRecorder` is a `ResponseWriter` that keeps what the handler wrote, in `rec.Code`, `rec.Header()`, and `rec.Body`. Your routes and middleware run for real, in microseconds.

Taskboard tests at three levels:

- Handler tests run the real HTTP layer and services over in-memory fakes of the stores, with no database.
- Repository tests run the real SQL on PostgreSQL, each test in a fresh schema of its own.
- One end-to-end test drives the whole stack through `httptest.NewServer`, a real server on a loopback port.

`go test -short ./...` skips the database tests for a fast loop, and CI runs everything with `-race`.

examples.title: A request helper
examples.prompt: Read `do`, the helper every Taskboard handler test sends its requests through.
examples.explanation: This helper is why each handler test is a line or two. `t.Helper()` makes a failure point at the test's line instead of the helper's. `httptest.NewRequestWithContext(t.Context(), ...)` gives the request a context that ends with the test (`t.Context` is new in Go 1.24). `a.handler` is the whole API from `NewServer`, middleware included, so these tests cover auth, problems, and headers along with each route.

examples.title: A table of bad requests
examples.prompt: Read `TestCreateTaskRejects`, a table-driven test. The output is `go test -short -count=1 -v -run TestCreateTaskRejects ./internal/api`.

    --- PASS: TestCreateTaskRejects/priority_4 (0.00s)
    --- PASS: TestCreateTaskRejects/priority_as_a_word (0.00s)

examples.explanation: Each row is one case: a name, a body, the expected status, and the field the problem must blame. `t.Run` makes each row a named subtest, so a failure says exactly which case broke, and `-run 'TestCreateTaskRejects/priority_4'` reruns just that one. Adding a case is one line. The test checks what a client relies on, the status and the field name, not the wording of messages, so improving a message never breaks it. All eight cases ran with no database at all.

examples.title: A test on a real database
examples.prompt: Read `TestDeleteCascades`, a repository test. The output is `go test -count=1 -v -run TestDeleteCascades ./internal/store`, run with `DATABASE_URL` pointing at PostgreSQL.
examples.output:
=== RUN   TestDeleteCascades
=== PAUSE TestDeleteCascades
=== CONT  TestDeleteCascades
--- PASS: TestDeleteCascades (0.07s)
PASS
ok  	example.com/taskboard/internal/store	0.075s
examples.explanation: A fake can't tell you whether your SQL is right. `ON DELETE CASCADE` is a promise the schema makes, so this test asks PostgreSQL itself. `testdb.New(t)` creates a fresh schema, applies every migration, and drops it in `t.Cleanup`, so tests can run in parallel with `t.Parallel()`, which is what the `PAUSE` and `CONT` lines show, without seeing each other's rows. After the repository call, the test checks the tables with a plain query, not with more repository code. Under `-short`, `testdb.New` skips the test.

recap:
- A middleware is a `func(http.Handler) http.Handler`, and the one wrapped last runs first.
- Wrap the `ResponseWriter` to see the status, and give the wrapper an `Unwrap` method.
- Pass `r.Context()` to every I/O call, keep request-scoped values under unexported key types, and give risky calls their own `context.WithTimeout`.
- Test handlers in memory with `httptest.NewRequest` and `httptest.NewRecorder`, in tables of named subtests.
- Test SQL against real PostgreSQL in a fresh schema per test, and skip those tests under `-short`.
